title: Kaapi Crosses the Ocean: South Indian Filter Coffee Opens Its Own American Cafes
excerpt: From East Atlanta to suburban Boston, a centuries-old brew in a steel tumbler is carving out a place beside the espresso machine.
body:
For decades, the Indian diaspora's morning ritual lived in home kitchens: degree coffee dripping slowly through a brass or steel filter, then poured back and forth between a tumbler and a dabarah until it foamed. Now that ritual is leaving the house. A small but growing wave of cafes across the United States is building entire businesses around kaapi — the South Indian filter coffee that most Americans have never heard of — and betting that the country ready to embrace flat whites and cortados is ready for this too.

## Context & Background

Coffee, not chai, is the daily drink across much of South India. Legend credits the seventeenth-century Sufi saint Baba Budan with smuggling a handful of beans home from Yemen after the Hajj, planting the seeds of a culture that today makes India the world's seventh-largest coffee producer. Roughly ninety percent of that coffee grows in the Western Ghats — Coorg, Chikkamagaluru, and Hassan in Karnataka, and the Nilgiris further south. The signature cup blends dark-roast beans with chicory, brews them through a two-chamber steel filter, and finishes with boiled milk and sugar or jaggery, hand-pulled into a froth.

That preparation is laborious and unmistakable, which is exactly what the new cafes are selling. Unlike a generation of Indian-American coffee shops that simply offered lattes alongside samosas, these places make kaapi the centerpiece.

## Current Developments

In East Atlanta, Praveena Sundarraj opened Raani Coffee on Moreland Avenue, where the steel filter is the star and the menu runs to gulab jamun lattes and biscuits flecked with curry leaves or masala and cheddar. In Woburn, Massachusetts, Kaapi & Co has built its identity around slow-brewed, chicory-blended filter coffee served the traditional way — hot, frothy, in a tumbler. The model is crossing borders too: a South Indian coffee brand is preparing to open its first Toronto cafe this fall, leading with filter coffee as its "hero" product alongside idlis and dosas on weekend brunch menus.

The momentum tracks a larger commercial shift. In India, chains like Hatti Kaapi have scaled filter coffee from a thirty-square-foot Bengaluru stall in 2009 to more than 110 outlets, including a first international store in London. India's domestic coffee consumption has climbed to roughly 91,000 tonnes a year, and its cafe market, valued at about $380 million in 2024, keeps growing at double-digit rates. The American cafes are riding that same wave of confidence — that authentic, milk-based South Indian coffee can scale without being diluted into something Eurocentric.

## Diaspora Impact

For South Indian families in the United States, these cafes are less a novelty than a homecoming. Filter coffee is bound up with memory — the smell of the morning kitchen, the specific clatter of the dabarah, the grandparent who insisted on getting the froth just right. A storefront that gets the ritual right offers something an Instant Pot and a mail-ordered filter cannot: a public, shared space where the drink is treated as worthy of a menu rather than an apology.

It also reframes the diaspora's relationship to coffee culture at large. For years, Indian Americans adapted to the espresso vocabulary of the country around them. A cafe that leads with kaapi flips the exchange — inviting non-Indian neighbors to learn a new word, a new vessel, and a new way to drink something they thought they already understood. The gulab jamun latte and the masala biscuit are gateways; the filter cup is the destination.

## What's Next

The test now is whether kaapi can move from cultural curiosity to durable category, the way Vietnamese ca phe sua da and Japanese pour-over once did. The economics are promising: filter coffee is cheap to make, distinctive enough to command attention, and backed by a deep supply chain in the Ghats. Expect more openings in metros with large South Indian populations — the Bay Area, Dallas, New Jersey, and the Seattle corridor — and growing pressure on specialty roasters to stock Indian single-origin and chicory blends.

If the pattern holds, the steel tumbler may become as legible on an American counter as the ceramic flat-white cup. For a diaspora that has spent decades explaining its food to others, watching strangers ask for a second cup of kaapi will feel like a small, frothy vindication.

**Sources:** 285 South (Raani Coffee profile); Kaapi & Co, Woburn MA; TasteToronto; Restaurant India (Hatti Kaapi).
